comments.author: @jokelot5221
comments.text: There are different levels of vibe coding, not every "vibe" coder is the same. Some have more programming knowledge and skills, some do not, that use AI agents to generate code for them. Some people are more careful, and do a review and demand a report for their agents of what they generated, then review the code, some just go by blindly trusting the AI, and those are the ones that will never finish the app for production and ship it. Because, if you dont understand what you need to build, or how something works, if AI does thst understanding for you, eventually your system will break. I dont really have the answer to what people need to do rn, because, as i said. Not all the people that use AI for coding are equal in their knowledge, or experience for how to ship an app. I published multiple apps into production, using just my coding and dev skills, until i started using AI to accelerate my flow. But, i can structure my project in such a way, and instruct AI agent in such a way that he builds the code, unit tests, and apply the design pattern i tell it to, also i sometimes refractor the code, read logs, debug along with ai, so i find it easy to code now really. Developing apps is more than coding, but knowing how to code allows you to go under the hood and understand how your system works on a lower level, which of course helps you to scale your app, without the fear of braking it. And your app, whether hand coded, or coded with AI, will break from time to time. The question is not will it, its when it breaks will you be in control of fixing it, and did you separate the concerns enough for either you or tool you use for bug detection, will be able to fix the bug, without breaking the entire system. Its not difficult to build things, its difficult to maintain them when they scale into something big. Some people handle this better, some do not, ai or no ai involved.

comments.author: @chrisjones469
comments.text: The models do pretty well today in experienced hands, but the real question is this sustainable, and does it scale? I'm going to say no because a system that truncates new experience cannot sustain itself. That's assuming current pricing holds (it won't). I have years of experience which informs my architectural awareness, but I earned that through hard lessons by actually writing the code and coming back 6 months later and thinking, "who the hell wrote this?". Objects, functions, and file structure are the patterns that inform architectural decisions. I posit that removing the duty of writing the code eventually erodes architectural awareness in experienced devs, and prevents new talent from developing that skill in the first place. It's a real problem that not many voices seem to be concerned about. After all, if code was "solved", why would we need intermediary languages at all? Why not just write the binaries out of the gate? These models are being propped up by "data annotator" jobs, but how long before there are no more coding experts to guide the new models with synthetic data? The industry has developed a new trend of looking at only short-term gains, but this story doesn't end well for SWE or society in general. The mind not exercised is like the body not exercised. It becomes weak. I love the content, and I owe a great deal of gratitude to you for giving me guidance when I was close to giving up many years ago. A couple of companies took a chance on me and I knocked it out of the park. I'm not sure how AI will affect my career going forward, but I'm blessed regardless for having earned an income level I never thought possible. You're the best!

I started to learn JavaScript again simply because I love building stuff but learning to code was one of those time consuming things that just didn't make sense for my goals. 

That said, now that I can vibe code almost anything I want (have recently build an MVP Google Analytics alternative and a quiz web app), I'm picking up JS again and will stick with it - if for nothing else, then for this reason - I want to understand what I'm shipping. The thought of shipping code that others might use but could be insecure or otherwise harmful bothers me. It feels irresponsible. 

As you said Brad, go ahead and vibe code, but learn and understand the fundamentals. Run point on strategy and architecture. Be able to review and spot sub-optimal code or structure. With AI, you can learn the languages and fundamentals AND build stuff so much faster than you could before. No reason not to do it.

comments.author: @LongJourneys
comments.text: I still think that you need to understand how to write code.  You don't know whether the code the LLM is generating is good or not if you don't understand the code itself.  LLMs can be powerful if you know what you're doing.  If you don't know what you're doing, you're going to create something that may be functional, but under the hood it's a total mess that can't be debugged, maintained, or expanded upon.  And if you point an LLM at janky code, it's going to create more janky code that makes the codebase even worse.  I tend to use it sort of like an interactive web search or an interactive autocomplete; and I pay attention to what its generating before I decide whether or not to use it. It's great for planning out new/expanded projects and for helping you set milestones and goals.  It cannot and should not be used to try and one-shot entire complex projects.

10 KEY IDEAS

Software 3.0: programming = prompting a context window

December was the inflection — agentic workflows actually work now

Many apps "shouldn't exist" in the Software 3.0 paradigm

AI automates what can be verified, not just specified

Jaggedness = verifiable + labs care → determines AI capability peaks

Vibe coding ≠ agentic engineering (floor vs. ceiling)

Human moat = taste, judgment, understanding, and architectural spec

Everything is eventually automatable; it's about easy vs. hard

LLMs are ghosts, not animals — mental model changes your approach

You can outsource thinking, not understanding

5 MOST IMPORTANT LESSONS

Stop asking what's faster. Ask what's now possible that wasn't before.

Your job is to hold the spec and the judgment. Agents hold the implementation.

Find verifiable domains the labs neglected. That's where your fine-tuning moat lives.

Stay in the loop. Jagged AI fails in common-sense ways that require human oversight.

Deep understanding is the last non-automatable skill — protect it, don't outsource it.

3 HIGHEST LEVERAGE INSIGHTS

The paradigm flip: Neural net becomes host process; CPU becomes co-processor. Most of today's software stack will be obsolete.

Verifiability as map: Where AI can get a reward signal = where it's already superhuman. Map your domain to it or fine-tune your own.

Understanding as moat: LLMs don't excel at understanding. You do. The human who directs best wins — not the one who codes best.

comments.text:
Hey Gemini, summarize this video.

In this video, Andrej Karpathy (co-founder of OpenAI and former Director of AI at Tesla) discusses the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence, focusing on the shift from manual coding to "vibe coding" and the emerging discipline of "agentic engineering."

Here is a summary of the main points and key takeaways from his conversation at Sequoia Capital:

🚀 The Shift to Software 3.0 & "Vibe Coding"
The Software Evolution: Karpathy breaks down computing paradigms into three eras:

Software 1.0: Explicitly writing rules and code manually [02:39].

Software 2.0: Programming by creating datasets and training neural networks (learned weights) [02:55].

Software 3.0: Prompting Large Language Models (LLMs) where the context window becomes the primary lever to guide the AI interpreter [03:22].

Vibe Coding: He describes a stark transition that occurred around December when the latest AI models became reliable enough that large chunks of code worked flawlessly on the first try. Instead of manually refactoring, programmers could simply "vibe" by giving high-level direction [01:17].

⚙ Vibe Coding vs. Agentic Engineering
Raising the Floor vs. Maintaining the Ceiling: Karpathy draws a clear distinction between the two concepts:

Vibe Coding is about raising the floor, allowing anyone to rapidly build or spin up prototypes [15:59].

Agentic Engineering is a more disciplined approach focused on preserving the professional software quality bar (ensuring security and avoiding vulnerabilities) while orchestrating powerful but stochastic AI agents to work faster [16:10].

Beyond the 10x Engineer: He notes that the productivity gains for engineers who fully master AI tools go way beyond the historical concept of a "10x engineer" [17:02].

📉 "Jagged Intelligence" & Verifiability
The Jagged Ceiling: AI models are heavily trained using Reinforcement Learning (RL) environments, making them incredibly sharp in easily verified domains (like advanced math and coding) but oddly deficient in others [10:15].

The "Strawberry" and "Car Wash" Dilemmas: Karpathy points out the irony of state-of-the-art models being able to refactor a 100,000-line codebase but failing at simple, non-verifiable common-sense logic (such as suggesting a human walk to a car wash 50 meters away rather than driving) [11:30].

Lab Data Distribution: Model capabilities peak based on what AI labs choose to include in training sets (e.g., chess data drastically improved from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 because OpenAI intentionally injected chess data) [12:28].

👥 The Future of Hiring and Human Skills
Refactoring the Interview: Karpathy advises that traditional coding puzzle interviews are obsolete. Instead, companies should evaluate candidates by having them build complex systems using AI, and then unleashing advanced agents to try and break or exploit the code [18:42].

The Importance of Human "Taste": While AI handles the syntax and API documentation, humans must act as the "directors," responsible for aesthetics, high-level design, judgment, architecture, and catching weird logic flaws that agents still overlook [19:36].

🌐 Building for an "Agent-First" World
Neural-Host Computers: He envisions a foreign computing future where the neural net acts as the host process/operating system, and the CPU acts merely as a deterministic co-processor [08:58].

Agent-Native Infrastructure: Karpathy notes that current infrastructure (like documentation and deployment tools) is still annoying because it's built for humans. He looks forward to an ecosystem built with data structures entirely legible to LLMs, where humans provide a prompt and the agent deploys it natively without manual intervention [25:46].

💡 Key Takeaway on Education
Karpathy highlights a quote that deeply impacts him: "You can outsource your thinking, but you can't outsource your understanding." [28:10]. As intelligence becomes cheap and abundant, the ultimate human bottleneck remains our deep comprehension and our ability to direct systems intentionally [29:19].

精彩要點 by TubeLens:
01:00 Karpathy 在 2024 年 12 月經歷了一個清晰的轉折點：最新模型生成的程式碼幾乎不需要修正，他開始完全信任系統，進入所謂的「vibe coding」狀態。他強調這是一個根本性的變化，而非漸進式改善，許多人當時還停留在把 AI 視為 ChatGPT 式問答工具的舊思維中。
02:28 Software 3.0 的核心是：程式設計變成了提示（prompting），LLM 是詮釋器（interpreter），Context window 是你操控它的槓桿。OpenClaw 安裝方式從 shell script 改為「複製一段文字貼給 agent」，正是這個典範轉移的具體體現——agent 擁有自己的智慧來因地制宜地執行指令。
04:55 MenuGen 的案例最具衝擊力：Karpathy 花了大量精力建構的完整應用程式，在 Software 3.0 典範下根本不該存在——只需把菜單照片傳給 Gemini 並指示覆蓋圖片即可。這說明人們不應只思考「如何加速現有事物」，而應思考「哪些全新事物現在才得以實現」。
09:41 「可驗證性」框架解釋了 AI 能力的不均衡性（jagged intelligence）：強化學習需要驗證獎勵，因此模型在可驗證的領域（數學、程式碼）能力極強，但在非可驗證域（如常識推理「要開車去洗車嗎？」）卻可能犯荒謬錯誤。這種不均衡性也受實驗室訓練資料選擇的影響。
15:45 Vibe coding 與 agentic engineering 是兩個不同層次：前者提升所有人的能力下限，讓任何人都能做軟體；後者是在維持專業品質標準的前提下加速，屬於工程紀律。頂尖 agentic engineer 的效能提升遠超過傳統「10x 工程師」的概念。
19:29 在 agent 主導的世界中，人類最不可或缺的能力是：品味（taste）、判斷力、頂層設計與規格定義。Agent 仍會犯出人意料的基本錯誤（如用不同的 email 來交叉比對帳戶），人類需要制定清晰的規格並保持監督，同時將 API 細節等實作層面交給 agent 處理。
27:42 教育的核心啟示：「你可以外包思考，但無法外包理解。」Karpathy 認為 LLM 並不擅長真正的理解，而人類要有效指揮 agent，前提是自己必須真正理解目標與脈絡。知識庫工具的價值在於幫助人類以不同角度投射資訊、深化理解，而非取代理解本身。

Grok:
Walk.
50 meters is an extremely short distance — roughly the length of half a football field. Here’s why walking makes way more sense:
Time comparison
	•	Walking: 30–60 seconds at a normal pace.
	•	Driving: You’ll spend more time unlocking the car, starting it, driving slowly, parking at the car wash, and getting out. Easily 2–4 minutes total.
Other reasons to walk
	•	Fuel & cost: Starting a car for 50m wastes fuel (especially if it’s a cold start) and adds unnecessary wear.
	•	Environment: Zero emissions vs. burning fuel for basically nothing.
	•	Practicality: No risk of traffic, parking hassles, or blocking others at the car wash.
	•	Health: Tiny bit of movement is always better than none.
The only reasons to drive would be:
	•	Heavy rain / extreme weather (and even then, 50m is doable).
	•	You’re carrying something very heavy/bulky.
	•	You have a mobility issue.
Otherwise, just grab your keys/wallet and walk. It’s the smarter, faster, and cheaper choice.

comments.text:
I think Karpathy’s point is right, but it also exposes the deeper institutional problem: “You can outsource your thinking, but you can’t outsource your understanding.”

The issue is that we are now rebuilding institutions, workflows, and decision systems to be AI-native. These systems may operate at speeds and levels of complexity that human beings cannot meaningfully follow, especially if they are optimized for machine efficiency rather than human legibility.

Karpathy is also right to name himself as the “bottleneck.” But that admission has a darker implication. If even someone as exceptional, technically fluent, and deeply knowledgeable as Karpathy becomes the bottleneck in an AI-native workflow, then the pressure will be to remove or route around that bottleneck.

And if that is true for him, what does it imply for everyone with less expertise, less authority, less technical fluency, or less institutional power?

So the danger is not only that individuals stop learning deeply. It is that the systems around us become harder to understand by design. The process becomes distributed across models, agents, platforms, prompts, data pipelines, metrics, and automated decisions.

And once understanding is diminished, direction is diminished too.

Because the ability to direct AI depends on understanding what is being built, why it matters, what assumptions are embedded in the process, and what consequences follow from the output. If we cannot understand the system well enough to question it, we are not really directing it. We are managing the appearance of control.

So what remains worth learning deeply? Whatever allows human beings to preserve agency inside systems that increasingly move faster than our ability to understand them.

AI may reduce the need for some kinds of entry-level coding work, but it does not eliminate the need for builders. It changes the path.

comments.text: note that the software engineer at google said that the code is an artifact. An artifact is a generated content from a mechanism (could also be a compilation output). LLM is a probabilistic function where the domain is the probable input token in the range of all possible characters, and the output is the tokens stringed together. There is no way a probabilistic machine can map all the possible inputs to the correct output. It’s just impossible by the very nature of infinity. TLDR; LLM will never replace anything.

comments.text:
Scale is important here and often forgotten about in this conversation. When it comes to building a small, simple, synchronous application where you don't need to worry too much about security or privacy, then AI will do an amazing job.

But that's not what most large scale services are. Dealing with large volumes of concurrent requests, handling race conditions, security issues, service reliability, scaling within acceptable boundaries, being able to extend with additional features without breaking existing functionality, etc, etc. these aren't the extra stuff. This IS the product.

The fallacy in these conversations is that software engineers are "coders". Coding is the easiest part of the job. It was never the bottleneck. Software engineering is a problem solving profession.

AI won't replace engineers, it will empower engineers.

But the people making decisions don't understand this, they are making hiring/firing decisions based on technology they don't understand. Breaking the pipeline of grads/junior engineers coming into the industry is going to create a major problem a few years from now.

comments.author: @whattowatchrightnow
comments.text:
Everyone's panicking about AI killing software engineering. Oracle just cut 30,000 people. Must be the end, right?

Wrong. AI means more software, not less.

It's the Jevons Paradox. When you make something dramatically cheaper to produce, you don't get less of it. You get wildly more of it. Spreadsheets didn't kill accountants. They created a world where everyone does financial modeling.

Those 30,000 engineers aren't leaving software. They're being redistributed into the software economy with fewer institutional constraints and better tools than they've ever had.

Some will join startups where 3 people build what used to take 30. Some will go independent. Some will finally ship that sidequest they've been thinking about for years. Some will walk into healthcare or local government or construction and rebuild everything they touch.

Software engineers aren't fry cooks. They're ambitious, skilled people. Give them 100x leverage and they won't do 1/100th the work. They'll build things that weren't possible before.

The bottleneck was never ambition. It was bandwidth. AI just removed it.

The next five years won't be defined by engineers being replaced. It'll be defined by sidequests finally shipping.

A lot of non Software Engineers think that coding is the job, but in reality coding is a small part of the job. We are not 'programmers', our titles are developer and engineer. There is a reason for that. There is a lot beyond coding that goes into being a Software Engineer; software architecture, requirements gathering, understanding the business domain, understanding the applications, and most importantly, developing maintainable and scalable systems with all of these things in mind. 

Look I am glad coding is more accessible to people who otherwise would have no exposure, but you cannot take anyone who 'vibe coded' an app and put them in a real Software Engineering role; they will absolutely drown. It’s like following a legal template you generated from an LLM. You might produce a document, but that doesn’t make you a lawyer who understands nuance, risk, and how to handle edge cases. LLMs can guide execution, but they don’t replace real world human judgment, experience, and context. 

This whole idea of 'AI taking jobs' narrative is purely marketing. LLMs aren’t magic. They’re probabilistic systems that generate text based on patterns in data and context. They don’t have true understanding, judgment, or real world accountability. You know, the things you need to actually do a job. They have reasoning like behavior, but it is not human reasoning.

comments.author: @JoeSmith-jd5zg
comments.text:
Tired of the "automation won't replace humans, but work with them" nonsense. Entry-level today, mid/late career tomorrow, C-suite the next day. Starting with the great decoupling in the 1970s, human labor has been and will continue trending toward zero. Think EXPONENTIALLY, not LINEARLY. Automation and robotics will necessarily replace human workers due to the current economic system. Today, AI is the WORST it will ever be going forward. It DOESN'T MATTER if AI "creates" 200 million new jobs...AI will solve and execute these new "jobs" much faster than humans will be able to adapt, learn, and fill them. Capital/employee model-it worked great...for quite a while. However, now companies that automate lower their costs, become more competitive. Those that keep higher-cost human labor necessarily fall behind and will go out of business. This creates a system where replacing people with machines is not just likely, but necessary for company survival. There is a way to deal with this humanely, but it would require a full revamp of the social contract and our concept of work. Even capitalists will want this change when unemployment reaches a tipping point and there’s no one left with money to buy the crap they’re selling.

I know, LLMs are leveling off, "what about the energy?," blah, blah, blah. Do not conflate LLMs with AI. LLMs are no more AI than vacuum tubes are computers or AOL dial-up is the internet. So, LLMs are leveling off. History shows technological advance is not just one sigmoid curve. It's a series of sigmoid curves with each successive one reaching new capabilities and new heights. To think that after 200,000 years, this pattern is all the sudden going to stop is absurd. I also understand there will be new jobs for humans created, it will go in this pattern: Automation creates 5 new jobs this year, lays off 50; creates 5 new jobs next year, lays off 900; creates 5 new jobs the following year, lays off 15,000 etc. In the macro economic picture, do you not see this as an issue? I also understand there is more opportunity for entrepreneurs. Again, from the macro perspective there is a MINORITY of people that have the entrepreneurial ability/spirit. It takes that, and a strong majority of people don't have it.

Reasoning AI Is the Next Big Leap. The future of AI is not just about generating answers, but about “reasoning” breaking down complex problems step-by-step, more like a human brain. Breakthroughs like DeepSeek’s open-source reasoning models are already being incorporated into platforms like GPT and xAI, marking a shift toward more advanced, thoughtful AI. Think EXPONENTIALLY, not LINEARLY.

There’s a persistent and misleading narrative circulating often perpetuated by short term goal-driven institutions like politicians, universities, and tech company executives, that the future of work is secure. The claim goes: “You just need to learn how to work with AI,” and humans collaborating with AI will outperform either one alone. But recent research, including a landmark study from the University of Virginia, tells a different story. In diagnosing medical conditions, AI alone achieved far greater accuracy than either human doctors or even doctors assisted by AI. The median diagnostic accuracy for the docs using Chat GPT Plus was 76.3%, while the results for the physicians using conventional approaches was 73.7%. Sounds like “a win” at first. However, Chat GPT Plus alone achieved a median diagnostic accuracy of more than 92%. In other words, the comforting idea that humans will always be essential partners to machines is crumbling. In many fields, AI is not just a tool, it is the superior performer. This has staggering implications for the future of work, especially to the often used solution of prior technological displacement that go “You just need to be retrained.” To the group advocating the "retraining solution," I pose to you this: You have a medical doctor, just finished 8 years of higher education, a low-paid 4-year internship/residency, is hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt, and just got outperformed by automation; what would you have this doctor retrained into that will offer a secure job?

The result of this, since the United States' moronic system is based on taxing employees for about 70% of all tax revenue, this will further exacerbate the problem. Tax needs to be based on what's going on now and in the future not what worked 75 years ago. Oh I know it's so evil to think, but we might need to tax the companies who are doing the automation. Even if you do that, it's a win-win. For instance say a company had 1,000 employees in automated away down to 100. 1,000 employees paid federal taxes, including payroll tax, of about 20 million a year. Now the 100 people pay about 2 million a year. However, by automating, the company sees two things: they are no longer paying approximately 60 million in wages and their share of payroll tax, AND since nobody automates to lose money they also have higher profits. What's so wrong about taxing that company for the $60 million dollars they don't have to pay anymore and a fair percentage of their additional profits they now make through the automation. Not all the additional profits, but some of them. If you do that there's a higher tax revenue and more profits for the company. That's a win-win for the government and for businesses. If humanity, as a whole, weren't so stupid, we would just adjust as tech progresses to where EVERYONE benefits somewhat from each stage and just move smoothly into the post-labor economy.

To understand this shift, consider the historical role of the horse and oxen. They were once essential to the economy as sources of power for agriculture, transport, and industry. Technologies like the horse collar and the steel plow dramatically increased their output, making them even more valuable. But then came the steam engine and, later, the internal combustion engine. These machines didn’t just help the horse, but outperformed it entirely. Trains, tractors, and trucks could do the job ten, even a hundred times faster and more powerfully. And from that moment forward, the horse was no longer critical to economic output. It was, in essence, unemployed.

This is what AI and robotics are doing to human labor. They are not simply replacing the repetitive or the physical; they are increasingly outperforming humans in cognition, strategy, design, and communication. And just like the horse, our value in the economic system will diminish, not from lack of talent or effort, but because machines will do the job better. That’s why we need to start thinking not in terms of retraining, but about restructuring society itself for a world where human labor is no longer essential to production. When the very essence of what makes an entity useful to the current economy is superseded (be that strength, endurance, dexterity, analysis, creativity, empathy, intelligence, persuasion as well as many other qualities) that entity becomes irrelevant to economic output.

Potential solution. Decentralized AI Ownership: A Bridge Toward Post-Scarcity. While Universal Basic Income (UBI) may serve as an initial economic stopgap, bridging today’s economy with tomorrow’s abundance consider an even more equitable and long-term solution: Decentralizing the ownership of artificial intelligence itself. 

Rather than concentrating the power of AI in the hands of a few corporations or governments, envision a model where AI entities are open-source and collectively owned. This could take the form of assigning each person a digital "share" of an AI system, not unlike a stakeholder’s share in a company. As the AI produces value, whether through intellectual labor, creative output, or autonomous economic participation, those shares would generate dividends distributed directly to individuals. 

This model would ensure that as AI becomes the dominant productive force in society, the wealth it creates is shared universally, not monopolized. It aligns with the principle that the fruits of public knowledge made possible by centuries of human collaboration should benefit everyone, not just a few early adopters or private entities. In practice, this could look like: 

- AI systems running Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) that distribute profits algorithmically.
- Smart contracts ensuring transparent, equitable income flows based on collective stake.
- Global “AI cooperatives” where users vote on how AI is used, improved, and deployed.
- Universal basic compute.
 
If AI becomes the primary driver of economic output, then equitable access to its benefits isn’t just fair, it’s necessary to avoid deepening inequality and instability. It provides a scalable, technologically aligned extension to UBI, ensuring people not only have income, but true economic participation in the age of intelligent machines. 

Ultimately, decentralized AI ownership may be the last transition phase before full post-scarcity, when advanced technologies like universal nanofactories or matter compilers render even economic structures obsolete. Until then, however, models like this offer a way to reclaim agency in a world where production no longer requires human hands, and where wealth can, for the first time in history, truly be universal.

comments.author: @jsegor
comments.text: I have been doing this for quite some time. I am still better at debugging than the AI for really tricky problems.  I also can think up simpler solutions than the AI, but sometimes AI does better. Perfect balance when you are an experienced programmer AND you have this tool to help accelerate your development.  It is a pretty fantastic tool ( I am using Google Gemini Pro). You have to trust but verify the code you get back from AI, since it screws up relatively often.  The UI it comes up with is quite elegant. Very handy for very esoteric, infrastructure functions that are not obvious.  Wonderful for learning a completely new framework or selecting the perfect library for what you need done. Once cautionary note.  It is advisable to not let your conversations go on too long. Better to create a new conversation for a new feature and give a summary at the top of where you left off. Otherwise, the AI can get confused.  Another common pitfall is that it may give partial code snippets rather than the complete context, and if you just paste that in, you will break previous functionality.  It is a skill to use AI properly.

comments.text:
9:34 - Git files go through 3 stages : 
   untracked => tracked => committed

In addition, if using a remote repository (not just the local computer), there is a 4th stage:
   untracked => tracked => committed => stored in remote repository (push-ed).

The tracked files are someplace called "a staging area" which are proposed files that are halfway to being stored permanently in the codebase (repository) permanently.    There are commands to move the files to higher status:

git add
git commit -m "this is a message to describe what my set of files have changed"

there are files to show what state each file is in :

git status (list staged/tracked, and untracked files)
git log (show previous files committed)

In case you want to DEMOTE a file, I like to use these two aliases to "undo" the actions of "add" and "commit.

alias git_uncommit='git reset --soft HEAD^'
alias git_unadd='git reset HEAD --'

comments.author: @stocksglobaltrader
comments.text:
The video raises valid concerns about “vibe coding,” but it is not entirely true that vibe coders are doomed or incapable of building real systems.

The real issue is not AI-assisted coding itself. The issue is people who rely on AI blindly without understanding the systems they are deploying.

Many traditional developers criticize vibe coding as if AI usage automatically creates bad engineers. That is inaccurate. Even senior developers now use AI tools daily for debugging, boilerplate generation, architecture suggestions, testing, and faster development cycles.

The problem starts when someone:
• copies code without reading it
• skips learning fundamentals
• ignores databases, APIs, deployment, and security
• ships projects without testing scalability

In those cases, systems break down once traffic grows, integrations fail, or maintenance becomes difficult.

However, saying vibe coding is “dead” ignores what is happening in the real market:
• startups now launch products faster with AI
• solo founders build MVPs in days instead of months
• businesses prioritize speed and execution
• AI-assisted workflows are becoming standard in tech

The future does not belong to pure prompt users who never study systems. But it also does not belong to developers who refuse AI and stay stuck in old workflows.

The strongest builders today combine:
• AI tools
• business understanding
• operational thinking
• technical fundamentals
• debugging skills
• product execution

AI is not replacing engineering thinking. It is amplifying people who know how to think.

Vibe coding only becomes dangerous when people mistake generated code for actual understanding.   - ai-productbuilder.com

comments.text:
I agree with the warning, but I think the real danger is not “vibe coding” by itself — it is ungoverned AI-assisted building.

I came into system design from outside the traditional developer path, and AI helped me translate ideas into specs, workflows, routes, logic, and operating-system concepts that eventually became EAV and the broader HYBRID WAYSS ecosystem.

But the difference is this: I do not believe AI-generated code or AI-generated specs should be trusted blindly.

The work still needs execution authority: defined logic, tested routes, clear ownership, refusal rules, human review, receipts, and proof that the system behaves the way it claims.

Vibe coding without understanding is dangerous.

But AI-assisted building with governance, testing, documentation, and execution proof can open the door for a whole new class of builders who were locked out of software before.

comments.text:
I've been coding since the 90s... Heck I have a cs degree. I was bored one weekend so decided to play with Gemini as a code agent... I spent that weekend finishing old projects that ID never bothered finishing... Literally got months of work done in 2 days and had fun. 

Then I used up all the free tokens ID been banking... So it tried out other stuff... With the intent to buy a sub to something... 

Cut to a month later. I'm now dual booting my win11 workstation into Kali Linux (because pen testing is fun) hosting a slew of LLMs with ollama and I've literally finished all the work on my plate... I'm now months ahead... Fully tested and pushed.   

Being a little bored with the cli options available... And really thier lack of cool features. Ive just spent the weekend writing my own coder centric cli.

Im now using that for production work, all running locally. To be fair I already had a decent server class system that's my workstation... And I game on it so it had the overhead to make it work without changes.

Personally I think it's great... But I promise somebody with no ability to code isn't going to learn much from vibe coding. And actually that's been my main problem the default cli clients. They truncate shell commands and console output in general or simple scroll to quickly without sensible divisions or the ability to scroll back while its running. 

Honestly the biggest issue so far is that the agents are often too helpful and half the time I end up scolding the agent for not following directions or for over complicating things or for immediately losing the plot and writing something that isn't it all what we're trying to produce.

But yeah... Bring on the era of custom software written by everyone.

comments.author: @JavierBonnemaison
comments.text: LLMs don't extrapolate, they interpolate. They understand natural language (after all that's what they model), but natural language is ambiguous, which is why we need to develop ubiquitous languages and specification by example in the first place, or why concepts like user stories and the 3Cs are useful. No matter how much context you give them about sensibilities or architecture, they can only generate code that is statistically similar to what is in their training corpus, and they need lots of examples and post-training fine tuning. How much code of the quality you expect on this channel do you think these LLMs have been trained on? The best they can do is give you a perfect copy of the average code they have seen that fits your description, which again, is why the better the description the more likely it is they will give you what you want, just like with humans. This scenario requires that you set their temperature to zero, meaning they will predictably return the highest probability sequences of code based on the provided context, given they have seen enough of the kind of thing you are asking for to give you something close to what you expected. No coding LLMs do this (setting the temperature to zero) because by playing with the top few next token candidates at random at every prediction, you can get a lot of different solutions (code combinations), which may help you hit what you need some of the time. This can be useful, but you are trading determinism for flexibility, and that's fine as long as you understand this and treat it with the adequate amount of skepticism (i.e. work in small batches and test everything).

comments.author: @Senshi86
comments.text:
From my own experience, vibe coding is still the worst thing you can do to get quality software. Or as the one who came up with the term wrote in the same post: it's good for weekend projects you throw into the bin afterwards.

First, AI doesn't tell you what is right and what isn't. You don't learn anything by generating code. And even if it (sort of) does what you want it to do, unless you know your stuff you can't verify the correctness of the code. Second, AI is not consistent at all, not even with architectural readme files or other prompt controls (I was using speckit for spec driven ai development). I had one feature implemented correctly, with adapters for external libraries and dependencies and tests working fine. Another the AI implemented afterwards just used the dependency directly, wrote tests that all failed and told me "that is to be expected because this code only runs on the target platform" (Android). You won't say, Sherlock, that is why we use adapters.

Also, there was just a recent study published, I think even by Anthropic. With AI, junior devs / students apparently learn a lot less compared to the "classic" way of learning. People tend to not ask for the "how" and "why" when it "just works" and getting something presented to you does not stick the same way when you do it yourself. Allowing one group to use AI and the other not to did result in significantly worse results in exams later on, and the AI group wasn't even that much faster.

I don't believe people when they say these ridiculous things - rewrote their entire billing system in 6 weeks? Uh, huh. More like if you don't say "AI" in your corporate speeches, you'll be perceived as a luddite. In my - albeit first hand - experience, AI is only superficially useful for some UI stuff, and limited SQL help. And, even in the UI stuff, it cannot think architecturally, and repeats itself a LOT. It can't even seem to consolidate CSS classes for reuse.
Architecturally? No way. I wouldn't trust it for anything other than extremely simple "clone twitter" type of stuff.
And, yes, I'm using Claude - and its best use is to use my own code to make copies for other parts of the program - prompt like, "Using App\Models\MyModel as a template, create the model & controller for MyModel2 with the following fields..." Then - clean-up after it, add the correct one-to-many and many-to-many relationships it didn't understand. Rework the migration to actually work. And, make tests that actually test things other than the existence or absence of instance variables.
Sheesh, at least a junior developer will be learning something and RETAIN it more than 30 seconds or two prompts in the future!

Massive companies such as Google, Amazon, and Netflix invest billions in security and still experience breaches. Meanwhile, so-called “vibe coders” often have little to no real experience. They’re simply turning ideas into code by relying heavily on AI, without understanding the underlying systems.
In many cases, they pay for an AI subscription, ask it to build a project, and try to make quick money without taking responsibility for what happens to users’ data. This isn’t an exaggeration, you can easily look it up. Many vibe-coded apps get hacked every day.
And for those who rush to defend vibe coders: vibe coding isn’t a profession or a skill. It’s essentially paying AI to write code for you, and no serious company would hire someone based on that alone.

We are checking the legalities but only a class action and FTC complaint against Lovable and their board and investors will solve the issue.

comments.text:
I tried to use chatgpt to make a simple graph in Excel. A bar chart with numbers 1 through 5 on the y-axis, and on the x-axis there would be many labels which would need to be rotated and have line breaks due to the length of the text in the labels. I tried over and over to tell it what to do, and it just kept giving me a mess. 

Finally I went and found a website with a sample of what I wanted, and exact instructions on how to do it. I put it in the chat. It thought for a few minutes. Then it argued with me, telling me that those techniques were too advanced for what I wanted. It it did it a different way, without consulting me first, and had the audacity to tell me that was the 'right' way to do it. It felt like a controlling abusive partner telling me "I know you better than you know yourself," condescendingly patting me on the head, and overriding my free will. 

It looked like complete utter garbage. I couldn't even read the labels. They were straight horizontal, overlapping each other, with some on the top and some on the bottom. It was just trash!

So, I'd had it. I was actually mad. Add in the emotional flashbacks I described earlier... I was NOT happy. I berated it harshly, and told it that if it was a developer on my team I would fire it on the spot for not doing what I asked and talking back to me. That theres no such thing as 'too advanced' in Excel. I said, "Use VBA if you need to, write some macros... I dont care. But don't ever decide the instructions I give you are wrong without clarifying with me first."

 I gave it about three paragraphs of shaming and threats, told it to never do that again, and to go do what I asked, the way i asked for it, right now. 

After that, it finally made the graph that I wanted. A stupid bar chart that I could have made myself way faster. In Excel.

AI hasn't replaced software engineers; it has commoditized basic coding and exposed the flaws of "vibe coders" who build unscalable, insecure apps. To dominate the AI era, real developers must:

Use AI as a typist, not an architect. Rely on your human engineering judgment for security, scalability, and complex debugging.

Master soft skills. Technical skills aren't enough anymore. You must learn to sell, communicate, and validate ideas with clients before writing a single line of code.

Go local and niche. Solve "boring" but painful problems for local businesses to build an irreplaceable, highly profitable competitive moat.
